items.title: Founding of the Qutb Shahi Dynasty & Golconda
items.body:
**In one line:** The Qutb Shahi dynasty was the Golconda kingdom founded in 1518 by a former Bahmani governor, and it ruled the Telugu Deccan for about 170 years.

**The story**

- The **Bahmani Sultanate**, the big Muslim kingdom of the Deccan, broke apart in the early 1500s into **five Deccan sultanates**.
- One of its provincial governors, **Quli Qutb Mulk** (full title Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk), was the **tarafdar** (provincial governor) of **Telangana**. As the Bahmani centre collapsed, he stopped obeying it and in **1518** ruled Golconda in his own name — the start of the **Qutb Shahi dynasty**.
- He was of **Turkoman origin**, born in **Persia**, and had earned the honorific **Qutb-ul-Mulk** ("pillar of the realm") as a Bahmani military chief.
- His line ruled from **1518 to 1687**, with the great granite fort of **Golconda** as its first capital.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Golconda is Andhra-Telangana's own medieval Muslim kingdom. Examiners test the founder, the year, the parent sultanate and the fact that it was one of five successor states.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Founder | Quli Qutb Mulk (Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk) |
| Year founded | 1518 |
| Earlier post | Bahmani governor (tarafdar) of Telangana |
| Origin | Turkoman, born in Persia; Shia Islam |
| First capital | Golconda hill fort |
| Dynasty span | 1518-1687 |

**Terms explained**

- **Bahmani Sultanate** = the first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan (founded 1347); it split into five sultanates in the early 1500s.
- **tarafdar** = the governor of a *taraf*, a province of the Bahmani kingdom.
- **Qutb-ul-Mulk** = an honorific title, "pillar of the realm", given to the founder as a military chief.
- **Deccan** = the plateau of southern-central India, south of the Narmada.

**Golconda fort and the diamond trade**

- **Golconda** was a massive **granite hill fort**, famed for its water system, granaries and acoustics (a clap at the entrance gate could be heard at the hill-top pavilion — a built-in warning signal).
- The kingdom's wealth rested on **diamonds**: the **Kollur mine** in the Krishna river valley produced legendary stones, including the **Koh-i-Noor** and the **Hope Diamond**.
- "Golconda diamond" is still used worldwide to mean a stone of exceptional purity.

**Don't confuse:** Quli Qutb Mulk (founded the **Qutb Shahis** of Golconda) with **Yusuf Adil Shah** (Bijapur) or **Ahmad Nizam Shah** (Ahmadnagar) — all three broke away from the same Bahmani parent, but into different sultanates.

**Remember it:** "1518 — a governor becomes a king at Golconda."

**TL;DR**

- Qutb Shahi dynasty founded 1518 by Quli Qutb Mulk, the Bahmani governor of Telangana.
- Founder was Turkoman, born in Persia; title Qutb-ul-Mulk.
- One of the five Deccan sultanates; ruled 1518-1687 from Golconda fort.
- Golconda's wealth came from Kollur-mine diamonds — the Koh-i-Noor and Hope Diamond.
keyPoints: Qutb Shahi dynasty founded 1518 by Quli Qutb Mulk (Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk), the Bahmani governor of Telangana.
Founder was of Turkoman origin, born in Persia; title Qutb-ul-Mulk earned under the Bahmanis.
Golconda was one of the five Deccan sultanates; dynasty ruled 1518-1687.
Golconda hill fort was famed for its water system, granaries and acoustics.
Golconda's wealth rested on diamonds from the Kollur mine — the Koh-i-Noor and Hope Diamond.
items.mnemonic: Five Deccan sultanates 'A-BABG': Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Bidar, Berar, Golconda.
items.source: Britannica & Wikipedia — Qutb Shahi dynasty; Golconda; Kollur Mine

items.title: Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah & Telugu Patronage
items.body:
**In one line:** Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (ruled 1550-1580) was the Telugu-loving fourth sultan, remembered as 'Malkibharam', who made Telugu a court language and built the Hussain Sagar lake.

**The story**

- Before he became king, **Ibrahim** spent about **seven years in exile at Vijayanagara**, the great Hindu empire to the south, as an honoured guest of its regent **Rama Raya**. There he absorbed the Telugu language and local culture.
- On taking the throne (**1550**), he was the **first of the dynasty to formally adopt the title 'Sultan'**.
- Out of genuine love for **Telugu**, he patronised Telugu poets and made it a court language alongside Persian — laying the foundation of Golconda's composite Deccani culture. Telugu tradition still fondly calls him **Malkibharam** (Ibharama Chakravarti).
- The **Hussain Sagar** lake/tank (also called Ibrahim Cheruvu) was constructed during his reign by **Hussain Shah Wali**, and the **Purana Pul** ('old bridge', 1578) was built across the **Musi river**.
- Telugu poets flourished under him: **Ponnaganti Telaganarya's Yayaticharitra** belongs to this milieu and is noted for being composed in **pure (achcha) Telugu** — Telugu without Sanskrit words.
- Golconda under Ibrahim joined the **confederacy of Deccan sultanates** that defeated **Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi), 1565** — the turning point that broke Vijayanagara's power.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** Ibrahim is the AP-specific face of the dynasty — his Telugu patronage and the Talikota battle are repeated exam points, and the 'first to use Sultan' and 'Malkibharam' facts appear in statement questions.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Reign | 1550-1580 (fourth sultan) |
| Telugu epithet | Malkibharam (Ibharama Chakravarti) |
| Before kingship | ~7 years' exile at Vijayanagara under Rama Raya |
| First | First Qutb Shahi to use the title 'Sultan' |
| Public works | Hussain Sagar / Ibrahim Cheruvu lake; Purana Pul bridge over the Musi |
| Telugu literature | Ponnaganti Telaganarya's Yayaticharitra (achcha Telugu) |
| Battle | Talikota (1565) — in the Deccan confederacy vs Vijayanagara |

**Terms explained**

- **Vijayanagara** = the powerful Hindu empire of the south (capital Hampi), where Ibrahim lived in exile.
- **Rama Raya** = the regent who effectively ran Vijayanagara and hosted Ibrahim.
- **confederacy of Deccan sultanates** = the alliance of Golconda, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Bidar.
- **Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi)** = the 1565 battle in which that alliance crushed Vijayanagara.

**Don't confuse:** **Ibrahim** (the Telugu-patron sultan, built Hussain Sagar) with his son **Muhammad Quli** (founded Hyderabad and the Charminar). Ibrahim once lived at Vijayanagara, yet later fought *against* it at Talikota.

**Remember it:** "Malkibharam loved Telugu" — Ibrahim is the Telugu-patron sultan.

**TL;DR**

- Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (r.1550-80), the fourth sultan, remembered as 'Malkibharam'.
- Lived in exile at Vijayanagara under Rama Raya; first Qutb Shahi to use 'Sultan'.
- Great patron of Telugu; built the Hussain Sagar lake.
- Fought in the Deccan confederacy at Talikota (1565) against Vijayanagara.
keyPoints: Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah (r.1550-80), the fourth ruler, is remembered as 'Malkibharam'.
He lived in exile at Vijayanagara under Rama Raya before taking the throne.
He was the first Qutb Shahi to formally use the title 'Sultan'.
A great patron of the Telugu language and its poets.
The Hussain Sagar lake (Ibrahim Cheruvu) dates to his reign.
Golconda fought in the Deccan confederacy at the Battle of Talikota (1565) against Vijayanagara.
Purana Pul bridge across the Musi river was built in his reign; Ponnaganti Telaganarya's Yayaticharitra (pure/achcha Telugu) belongs to his milieu.
items.mnemonic: 'Malkibharam loved Telugu' — Ibrahim = the Telugu-patron sultan.
items.source: Wikipedia — Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah; Battle of Talikota

items.title: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, Hyderabad & the Charminar
items.body:
**In one line:** Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (ruled 1580-1611), the fifth sultan, founded the city of Hyderabad in 1591, built the Charminar, and was a pioneering poet.

**The story**

- By the late 1500s the hilltop fort of Golconda was overcrowded and short of water. So in **1591** the fifth sultan, **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah**, laid out a brand-new planned grid-city on the plains nearby — **Hyderabad**.
- At its centre he raised the **Charminar (1591)**, a square monument with four grand arches and four minarets, now the emblem of the city and of Telangana.
- Tradition links the city's original name **Bhagyanagar** to **Bhagmati**, his beloved (later titled Hyder Mahal), from whom the name 'Hyderabad' is popularly derived.
- He was himself a **poet**: his **Kulliyat** (collected poems) is regarded as the **earliest known diwan in Urdu/Deccani**, and he also composed in Persian and Telugu.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** '1591 + Charminar + Hyderabad + Muhammad Quli' is the single most-asked cluster in this topic, and his Kulliyat is a favourite literature fact.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Reign | 1580-1611 (fifth sultan) |
| City founded | Hyderabad, 1591 (first named Bhagyanagar) |
| Monument | Charminar, 1591 |
| Naming legend | Bhagmati / Hyder Mahal to Bhagyanagar to Hyderabad |
| Literary first | Kulliyat — earliest known Urdu/Deccani diwan |

**Terms explained**

- **Charminar** = "four minarets"; a square gateway-monument with four arches, built 1591.
- **diwan** = a poet's collected works; a **Kulliyat** is a complete collection.
- **Deccani (Urdu)** = the early form of Urdu that grew in the Deccan, mixing Persian with local speech.
- **Bhagyanagar** = "city of fortune", the city's original name.

**Don't confuse:** **Muhammad Quli** (founded Hyderabad/Charminar, fifth sultan) with his father **Ibrahim** (the fourth sultan, the Telugu patron). The city and the Charminar share one birth year — **1591**.

**Remember it:** "1591 = Hyderabad + Charminar" — the city and its icon share a birth year.

**TL;DR**

- Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (r.1580-1611) founded Hyderabad in 1591.
- Built the Charminar (1591), symbol of Hyderabad and Telangana.
- City first called Bhagyanagar, linked by tradition to Bhagmati.
- His Kulliyat is the earliest known diwan (collected poems) in Urdu/Deccani; he wrote in Persian and Telugu too.
keyPoints: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (r.1580-1611) founded Hyderabad in 1591.
He built the Charminar (1591), now the symbol of Hyderabad and Telangana.
The city was first called Bhagyanagar, linked by tradition to Bhagmati.
His Kulliyat is the earliest known diwan (collected poems) in Urdu/Deccani.
He also composed poetry in Persian and Telugu, reflecting Golconda's composite culture.
items.mnemonic: '1591 = Hyderabad + Charminar' — the city and its icon share a birth year.
items.source: Wikipedia — Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah; Charminar; Hyderabad

items.title: Madanna, Akkanna & the Fall of Golconda (1687)
items.body:
**In one line:** The last sultan, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, ran an inclusive court with Brahmin chief ministers, but Golconda fell to Aurangzeb's Mughals in 1687.

**The story**

- **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** (ruled 1672-1687) was the **eighth and last** Qutb Shahi ruler, remembered as a tolerant, inclusive sovereign.
- He made the **Brahmin brothers Madanna and Akkanna** his chief ministers; together they ran the **administration, tax collection and treasury** of Golconda.
- **Kancherla Gopanna (Bhakta Ramadasu)**, who built the Rama temple at **Bhadrachalam**, was their nephew and served as a Qutb Shahi **tahsildar** (revenue official). He is celebrated as the composer of Telugu devotional songs, the **Ramadasu keertanas**.
- The rise of powerful Hindu ministers alarmed Mughal and Muslim-noble opinion. **Aurangzeb**, already expanding into the Deccan, invaded. The ministers were killed, and after a long siege **Golconda fell in 1687**, reportedly through the **treachery of an insider** who opened a fort gate rather than by direct assault.
- Golconda was **annexed to the Mughal empire**; **Tana Shah was imprisoned at Daulatabad**, where he died in 1699, ending the dynasty.

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The fall of Golconda (1687, Aurangzeb, betrayal) and the Madanna-Akkanna-Ramadasu trio are standard match and statement material, and show Golconda's composite Hindu-Muslim culture.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Last ruler | Abul Hasan Tana Shah (r.1672-87), eighth sultan |
| Chief ministers | Brahmin brothers Madanna & Akkanna |
| Devotee-official | Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna), Bhadrachalam |
| Conqueror | Aurangzeb, after an ~8-month siege |
| How it fell | Insider's treachery opened a gate |
| Fate of Tana Shah | Imprisoned at Daulatabad; died 1699 |

**Terms explained**

- **tahsildar** = a revenue/administrative officer in charge of a sub-district.
- **chief minister** = the head of the royal administration (here, running tax and treasury).
- **annexed** = absorbed into another state (Golconda into the Mughal empire).
- **Daulatabad** = the hill fort (in modern Maharashtra) used as a Mughal state prison.

**Don't confuse:** **Madanna and Akkanna** were **ministers of Tana Shah** (late 1600s), not court poets of Ibrahim; and Tana Shah was **imprisoned**, never restored as a vassal.

**Remember it:** "1687 — Aurangzeb takes Golconda by a traitor's gate, not a frontal attack."

**TL;DR**

- Abul Hasan Tana Shah (r.1672-87) was the eighth and last Qutb Shahi ruler.
- Brahmin brothers Madanna and Akkanna ran his tax and treasury; Bhakta Ramadasu was their nephew and a tahsildar.
- Aurangzeb besieged and captured Golconda in 1687 through an insider's treachery.
- Golconda annexed to the Mughals; Tana Shah died a prisoner at Daulatabad (1699).
keyPoints: Abul Hasan Tana Shah (r.1672-87) was the eighth and last Qutb Shahi ruler.
Brahmin brothers Madanna and Akkanna served as his chief ministers, running tax and exchequer.
Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna) of Bhadrachalam was their nephew and a Qutb Shahi tahsildar.
Aurangzeb besieged and captured Golconda in 1687, aided by an insider's treachery.
Golconda was annexed to the Mughal empire; Tana Shah died a prisoner at Daulatabad (1699).
items.source: Wikipedia — Abul Hasan Qutb Shah; Madanna and Akkanna

items.title: Qutb Shahi Culture, Tombs & the Asaf Jahi Succession
items.body:
**In one line:** The Qutb Shahis left a composite Deccani culture and great monuments, and after they fell, Hyderabad passed to the Mughals (1687) and then to the Asaf Jahi Nizams (1724).

**The story**

- The Qutb Shahis fostered a distinctive **Deccani Indo-Islamic architecture** that blended Persian form with local Hindu craft — the **Charminar**, the grand **Makkah Masjid** (begun by Muhammad Quli around 1614, completed under the Mughal emperor **Aurangzeb in 1694**), and the palaces of Golconda.
- Their burial ground, the **Qutb Shahi Tombs** at **Ibrahim Bagh** near Golconda, is a garden necropolis of domed royal tombs.

**Monuments at a glance**

| Monument | Association |
| --- | --- |
| Golconda Fort | Granite hill citadel and early capital |
| Charminar | Founded 1591 as the centrepiece of Hyderabad |
| Makkah Masjid | Grand mosque begun by Muhammad Quli, finished under Aurangzeb |
| Qutb Shahi Tombs | Necropolis of the dynasty at Ibrahim Bagh |
- Court culture was **composite Deccani**: Persian and Deccani Urdu alongside strong **Telugu** patronage, seen in Ibrahim's Telugu court and Muhammad Quli's Telugu verse.
- After the **1687** Mughal annexation and the later weakening of the Mughals, the Deccan viceroy **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I** (Mir Qamaruddin Khan) founded the **Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty** of Hyderabad in **1724**.
- The Asaf Jahis, patrons of Indo-Persian culture, ruled **Hyderabad State** until its accession to India in **1948** (seven Nizams in all).

**Why it matters / why it is asked:** The monuments (and who built/finished them) and the succession line over Hyderabad are frequent match and sequence questions.

**Picture it**

| Who holds Hyderabad | From |
| --- | --- |
| Qutb Shahis | 1518-1687 |
| Mughals | 1687 (Aurangzeb's conquest) |
| Asaf Jahi Nizams | 1724-1948 |

**Terms explained**

- **Deccani Indo-Islamic style** = Deccan architecture mixing Persian domes and arches with local Hindu craft.
- **necropolis** = a "city of the dead", a large group of monumental tombs.
- **Makkah Masjid** = a huge mosque near the Charminar; by tradition some bricks use soil from Mecca.
- **Asaf Jahi (Nizam) dynasty** = the line of rulers of Hyderabad State from 1724 to 1948.

**Don't confuse:** The **Makkah Masjid** was **begun by the Qutb Shahis** (c.1614) but **completed by the Mughals** under Aurangzeb (1694) — two dynasties, one mosque. The **Qutb Shahi Tombs** (royal graves) are not the same as **Golconda fort** (the citadel).

**Remember it:** Succession over Hyderabad — "Qutb Shahi to Mughal (1687) to Asaf Jahi (1724)".

**TL;DR**

- Qutb Shahi architecture = Deccani Indo-Islamic: Charminar, Makkah Masjid, Golconda.
- Makkah Masjid begun c.1614 by Muhammad Quli, completed under Aurangzeb in 1694.
- Qutb Shahi Tombs stand at Ibrahim Bagh near Golconda — the dynasty's necropolis.
- Hyderabad passed Qutb Shahi to Mughal (1687) to Asaf Jahi Nizams (1724-1948).
keyPoints: Qutb Shahi architecture = Deccani Indo-Islamic style: Charminar, Makkah Masjid, Golconda.
Makkah Masjid was begun c.1614 by Muhammad Quli and completed under Aurangzeb in 1694.
The Qutb Shahi Tombs stand at Ibrahim Bagh near Golconda — the dynasty's necropolis.
Court culture was composite Deccani: Persian, Deccani Urdu and strong Telugu patronage.
After the Mughal decline, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I founded the Asaf Jahi dynasty of Hyderabad in 1724.
The Asaf Jahis ruled Hyderabad State until its accession to India in 1948.
items.mnemonic: Succession over Hyderabad: Qutb Shahi → Mughal (1687) → Asaf Jahi (1724).
items.source: Wikipedia — Qutb Shahi tombs; Makkah Masjid, Hyderabad; Asaf Jahi dynasty

items.title: The Eight Qutb Shahi Rulers and the Mughal Squeeze (1518–1687)
items.body:
### The Eight Qutb Shahi Rulers and the Mughal Squeeze (1518–1687)

**In one line**
Eight sultans ruled Golconda for 169 years; from 1636 they were Mughal tributaries, and their last fifty years are a story of Shah Jahan, Mir Jumla and Aurangzeb.

**The story**
The founder **Sultan Quli** (**1518–1543**) was murdered at the instigation of his son **Jamsheed** (1543–1550). After the child **Subhan**, **Ibrahim** (**1550–1580**) and **Muhammad Quli** (**1580–1611**) were the great builders, followed by **Sultan Muhammad** (1611–1626). **Abdullah** (1626–1672) signed the **Deed of Submission** with Shah Jahan in **1636**. His wazir **Mir Jumla** defected to the Mughals, and in **1656** Aurangzeb besieged Golconda until Abdullah paid an **indemnity**. The last king, **Tana Shah** (**1672–1687**), lost Golconda when **Abdullah Khan Pani** opened a gate; **Abdur Razzaq Lari** fought on, and the **Fateh Darwaza** recalls Aurangzeb's entry.

#### The eight rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk** | 1518–1543 | 'Bade Malik'; murdered (1543) at the instigation of his son **Jamsheed** |
| **2. Jamsheed Quli** | 1543–1550 | Took the throne after the murder; Ibrahim fled to Vijayanagara |
| **3. Subhan Quli** | 1550 | Child king, soon replaced by Ibrahim |
| **4. Ibrahim Quli** | 1550–1580 | 'Malkibharam'; Talikota; Hussain Sagar |
| **5. Muhammad Quli** | 1580–1611 | Hyderabad and Charminar (1591) |
| **6. Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah** | 1611–1626 | Muhammad Quli's nephew and son-in-law |
| **7. Abdullah Qutb Shah** | 1626–1672 | Accepted Mughal overlordship (1636) |
| **8. Abul Hasan Tana Shah** | 1672–1687 | Last ruler; Madanna and Akkanna |

#### Golconda and the Mughals

| Event / person | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Deed of Submission** | **1636** | Abdullah accepted **Shah Jahan**'s overlordship, read the khutba in his name and paid tribute |
| **Mir Jumla** | 1650s | Persian diamond magnate and Golconda **wazir**; defected to the Mughals; said to have given Shah Jahan the Koh-i-Noor |
| **Siege of 1656** | **1656** | Aurangzeb (viceroy) besieged Golconda; Abdullah paid an **indemnity** and gave a daughter in marriage |
| **Abdullah Khan Pani** | 1687 | Afghan officer who opened a gate to the Mughals — the insider's treachery |
| **Abdur Razzaq Lari** | 1687 | Noble who fought to the end against the Mughals |
| **Fateh Darwaza** | 1687 | 'Victory Gate' of Golconda, named after Aurangzeb's entry |

**Don't confuse**
- **Muhammad Quli** (5th, 1580–1611: Hyderabad, Charminar) ≠ **Sultan Muhammad** (6th, 1611–1626) ≠ **Sultan Quli** (founder).
- **Deed of Submission (1636)** was with **Shah Jahan**; the **annexation (1687)** was by **Aurangzeb**.
- **Mir Jumla** was a Golconda minister who joined the Mughals — not a Qutb Shahi king.

**TL;DR**
- Sultan Quli 1518–43 → Jamsheed 1543–50 → Subhan 1550 → Ibrahim 1550–80 → Muhammad Quli 1580–1611 → Sultan Muhammad 1611–26 → Abdullah 1626–72 → Tana Shah 1672–87.
- Deed of Submission with Shah Jahan, 1636; Mir Jumla defected; Aurangzeb besieged Golconda in 1656.
- 1687: Abdullah Khan Pani opened a gate; Abdur Razzaq Lari resisted; Fateh Darwaza.
keyPoints: Sultan Quli (1518–1543) was murdered at the instigation of his son Jamsheed (1543–1550).
Ibrahim Quli ruled 1550–1580 and Muhammad Quli 1580–1611; Abdullah Qutb Shah ruled 1626–1672 and Tana Shah 1672–1687.
Abdullah signed the Deed of Submission with Shah Jahan in 1636.
Mir Jumla, the Golconda wazir, defected to the Mughals; Aurangzeb besieged Golconda in 1656.
In 1687 Abdullah Khan Pani opened a gate to the Mughals; the Fateh Darwaza recalls the victory.

items.title: Golconda Trade, Literature and Monuments — the Details
items.body:
### Golconda Trade, Literature and Monuments — the Details

**In one line**
Golconda was a trading kingdom (Masulipatnam, diamonds, chintz) with a two-language culture (Telugu and Dakhini Urdu); exams match ports, foreigners, poets and buildings.

**The story**
Golconda's port was **Masulipatnam**, where the **Dutch** (1605) and **English** (1611) built factories, and in **1632** Abdullah granted the English the **Golden Farman**. The **French** jeweller **Tavernier** described its diamonds, and **kalamkari** cloth went abroad. Telugu verse flourished — **Addanki Gangadhara** wrote the **Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu** for Ibrahim and **Rudrakavi** the **Nirankusopakhyanamu** — and so did Dakhini: **Wajhi** wrote **Qutb Mushtari** and **Sabras**, **Ghawwasi** the **Saif-ul-Muluk**, and Muhammad Quli signed as **Ma'ani**. The fort grew from the Kakatiya **mud fort** of **Golla Konda**. The Charminar is said to mark the end of a **plague**; **Mir Momin** (the **Peshwa**) planned the city; the **Badshahi Ashurkhana** served **Muharram**; there are also the **Char Kaman**, the **Toli Masjid** and **Hussain Shah Wali**'s tank. The monuments are on UNESCO's **tentative list**, and the tombs were restored by the **Aga Khan Trust**.

#### Ports, Europeans and trade

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Masulipatnam** | Chief port of Golconda (Machilipatnam) |
| **Dutch factory** | At Masulipatnam, **1605** |
| **English factory** | At Masulipatnam, **1611** (also Petapoli/Nizampatnam) |
| **Golden Farman** | **1632** — Abdullah Qutb Shah let the English trade from Golconda ports for a fixed yearly payment |
| **Tavernier** | **French** jeweller; visited the Golconda (Kollur) mines in the 17th c. |
| **Textiles** | Masulipatnam chintz and **kalamkari** — major exports |

#### Telugu and Dakhini literature

| Writer / work | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Addanki Gangadhara** | **Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu**, dedicated to Ibrahim Qutb Shah |
| **Kandukuri Rudrakavi** | **Nirankusopakhyanamu**; patronised by Ibrahim |
| **Mulla Wajhi** | **Sabras** (1635) — first great Dakhini Urdu prose work |
| **Qutb Mushtari** | Wajhi's Dakhini masnavi (1609) on Muhammad Quli's romance |
| **Pen-name** | Muhammad Quli wrote as '**Ma'ani**' |
| **Ghawwasi** | **Saif-ul-Muluk** wa Badi-ul-Jamal (Dakhini masnavi) |

#### Monuments of Golconda and Hyderabad

| Monument | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Golconda Fort** | From '**Golla Konda**' (shepherd's hill); a Kakatiya **mud fort**, ceded by Kapaya Nayaka to the Bahmanis, rebuilt in granite by the Qutb Shahis |
| **Charminar — why** | Tradition: to mark the end of a **plague**; granite and lime mortar, four arches and four minarets (56 m) |
| **Mir Momin Astarabadi** | **Peshwa** (prime minister) of Muhammad Quli; planned Hyderabad |
| **Badshahi Ashurkhana** | 1594; royal hall for Shia **Muharram** mourning |
| **Char Kaman** | Four ceremonial arches near the Charminar (1592) |
| **Toli Masjid** | 1671; by Mir Musa Khan in Abdullah's reign |
| **Hussain Sagar** | Built **1562** by **Hussain Shah Wali** in Ibrahim's reign |
| **UNESCO** | Golconda Fort, Qutb Shahi Tombs and Charminar — on the **tentative list** (2010), not yet inscribed |
| **Restoration** | Qutb Shahi Tombs restored by the **Aga Khan Trust** for Culture with the Telangana government |

**Don't confuse**
- **Golden Farman** (1632, Golconda, Abdullah Qutb Shah) ≠ the Mughal farman of 1717 (Farrukhsiyar, to the English in Bengal).
- **Sabras** (Wajhi, prose, 1635) ≠ **Kulliyat** (Muhammad Quli, poetry diwan).
- Golconda monuments are only on UNESCO's **tentative** list; Hampi (1986) and Ramappa (2021) are inscribed sites.

**TL;DR**
- Masulipatnam: Dutch 1605, English 1611; Golden Farman 1632; Tavernier (French).
- Telugu: Addanki Gangadhara (Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu), Kandukuri Rudrakavi (Nirankusopakhyanamu).
- Dakhini: Wajhi — Qutb Mushtari, Sabras (1635); Ghawwasi — Saif-ul-Muluk; Muhammad Quli = Ma'ani.
- Golconda = Golla Konda (Kakatiya mud fort); Charminar — plague tradition; Mir Momin (Peshwa); Badshahi Ashurkhana (Muharram); UNESCO tentative list.
keyPoints: Masulipatnam was the chief Golconda port; the Dutch (1605) and English (1611) set up factories there.
Abdullah Qutb Shah granted the English the 'Golden Farman' in 1632; the French jeweller Tavernier described Golconda diamonds.
Addanki Gangadhara dedicated the Tapati Samvaranopakhyanamu to Ibrahim Qutb Shah; Kandukuri Rudrakavi wrote the Nirankusopakhyanamu.
Mulla Wajhi wrote the Qutb Mushtari and the Sabras (1635), the first great Dakhini prose work.
Golconda takes its name from 'Golla Konda'; the Charminar is said to mark the end of a plague; Golconda Fort, Qutb Shahi Tombs and Charminar are on UNESCO's tentative list.

items.title: For Mains — Qutb Shahis of Golconda
items.body:
**In one line:** For APPSC Mains Paper-II (AP medieval history, 1000-1565 and the Deccan sultanates), the Qutb Shahis are the case study of a regional Muslim state that built a lasting Telugu-Persian composite culture.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Rise | Break-up of the Bahmani Sultanate; Quli Qutb Mulk's independence at Golconda (1518); near-impregnable fort + diamond revenue |
| Administration | Taraf-based governance; inclusive court — Brahmin ministers Madanna & Akkanna; Telugu officials such as Ramadasu |
| Culture | Deccani Indo-Islamic architecture; Telugu patronage; composite identity centred on Hyderabad |
| Economy | World diamond emporium (Kollur mine); Masulipatnam port and Indian Ocean trade |
| Significance | Gave Hyderabad and modern Telangana's cultural core; bridged Persianate and Telugu worlds |
| Decline / limitations | Court factionalism; noble resentment of Hindu ministers; collapse before Aurangzeb (1687) |

**Data points / names to quote**

- **1518** founding; **1565** Talikota (Deccan confederacy vs Vijayanagara); **1591** Hyderabad and Charminar; **1687** fall to Aurangzeb; **1724** Asaf Jahi succession.
- **Ibrahim Quli ('Malkibharam')** — Telugu as court language; **Muhammad Quli** — Kulliyat, the earliest Urdu/Deccani diwan.
- **Ponnaganti Telaganarya's Yayaticharitra** (pure/achcha Telugu); **Bhakta Ramadasu's** Bhadrachalam keertanas.
- Monuments: **Charminar, Makkah Masjid (1614-1694), Qutb Shahi Tombs, Golconda fort** — now on Hyderabad's UNESCO tentative list.

**The AP angle:** Golconda is Andhra-Telangana's own medieval kingdom; its Telugu-Persian synthesis and Hyderabad's founding are the regional heart of the Deccan-sultanate story and ideal AP-specific examples.

**Use in answers**

- Example: contrast Golconda's inclusive administration (Madanna-Akkanna) with the sectarian turn under Aurangzeb to show why regional pluralism mattered.
- Quote: Muhammad Quli's Deccani verse celebrating Hyderabad shows a ruler writing in the people's language.
- Diagram idea: a timeline strip 1518, 1565, 1591, 1687, 1724 for rise-to-succession.
keyPoints: Mains Paper-II clause: AP medieval history and the Deccan sultanates (Qutb Shahis).
Frame rise-administration-culture-economy-significance-decline for a balanced answer.
Quote 1518 / 1565 Talikota / 1591 Hyderabad-Charminar / 1687 fall / 1724 Asaf Jahi.
Telugu-Persian composite culture: Ibrahim 'Malkibharam', Muhammad Quli's Kulliyat, Yayaticharitra, Ramadasu.
AP angle: Golconda is the regional core of the Deccan story and of modern Hyderabad/Telangana.
